title: Steve Eisman's Masterclass on the 2008 Financial Crisis (Part One) | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 38
summary: Eisman explains the crisis through leverage, deteriorating mortgage quality, concentration of exposures and derivative connections. His strongest analytical lessons are that leverage can masquerade as operating skill, historical loss models can fail when underwriting changes, and like-aged loan vintages reveal deterioration hidden by aggregates. Primary research supports these mechanisms. His account overstates a universal risk-weighting explanation and misdescribes typical subprime introductory rates. Loan-level evidence also complicates his reset-centered causal chain. The blanket claim that real household incomes stopped growing in the early 1990s is contradicted by Census data.
assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
framework_points: Decompose ROE into asset profitability and leverage.
Treat estimated loan losses as uncertain costs rather than immediately known margins.
Question historical risk weights when underwriting changes.
Compare loan vintages at equal seasoning and account for tax-refund seasonality.
Choose a short instrument with manageable liquidity, borrow costs and capacity.
tools_and_charts: Illustrative banks with $1 billion equity and 1x, 10x and 100x assets/equity
ROA, ROE and risk-weighted capital ratios
Historical bank leverage and subprime origination volumes
Low/no-documentation share and hybrid mortgage refinancing
Monthly securitization delinquency, repossession and loss reports by vintage
transcript_cautions: The opening montage repeats later material.
Illustrative bank balance sheets expressly omit liquidity and hold ROA constant.
He calls 2000 a recession year and gives simplified industry chronology; incidental chronology is not used to judge the investment thesis.
The repeated 3% initial subprime rate is load-bearing in the refinancing explanation and is preserved rather than silently corrected.

claims.claim: The crisis combined excessive leverage, a collapsing mortgage asset class, concentrated exposure at systemic institutions and opaque derivative links.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Trace losses, funding and counterparty exposures across major institutions.
claims.reason: Primary research and the commission investigation support the interacting leverage, common-exposure and funding mechanisms. This is a useful broad diagnosis, not proof that these exhaust every cause.

evidence.title: Financial Statistics for the United States and the Crisis
evidence.finding: Research identifies leverage, short-term funding and shared exposures as core vulnerabilities. Loan-vintage data show worsening early-payment defaults, reaching about 8% for 2007 loans within one year, and explain why aggregate data can conceal risk.

evidence.title: Financial Crisis Inquiry Report, findings and chapters 4, 6, 7, 13
evidence.finding: Investigative evidence documents fragile leverage/funding, fee and ROE incentives, deteriorating underwriting, and securitization dependence. Pages 61-64 describe pay incentives; pages 89 and 125 describe the origination chain; page 281 reports Bear near 38:1 and balance-sheet window dressing. Findings are not proof of a single exclusive cause.

claims.claim: Lenders do not know eventual loan losses when they originate credit, so apparent profitability depends on uncertain loss estimates.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare origination loss estimates with vintage lifetime defaults and recoveries.
claims.reason: Future defaults and recoveries are unknown at origination. Replacing an expected loss with the realized loss can change reported lifetime profitability, even with unchanged contractual interest.
claims.next_check: Obtain primary evidence matching the stated metric, period and conditions before assigning an outcome grade.

claims.claim: For consistent income, asset and equity definitions, return on equity equals return on assets multiplied by assets-to-equity leverage.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Reconcile average balances and capital definitions before applying the identity.
claims.reason: (Net income/assets)*(assets/equity)=net income/equity, for nonzero assets and equity with matching measurement periods. This is an identity, not an assurance that ROA remains constant when leverage changes.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

claims.reason: In the stated examples ROA is fixed after deposit interest expense. Increasing assets relative to unchanged equity therefore increases ROE. Real funding costs and risk can alter ROA.

claims.test: Inspect incentive contracts, deferred compensation, clawbacks and actual leverage decisions.
claims.reason: The investigation documents asymmetric pay and ROE-based rewards that encouraged leverage and short-term risk. It does not establish that regulators are the only possible restraint.

evidence.finding: Describes Basel I mortgage capital rules, proposed Basel II internal default/loss estimates, and separate non-risk-weighted leverage limits. Regulatory capital is not simply common equity and risk weights were not all delegated to external rating agencies.

claims.claim: Real incomes for most Americans stopped increasing in the early 1990s and remain stagnant in that sense today.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Specify household versus individual income and measure the relevant distribution over the claimed period.
claims.reason: Census real median household income rose from $64,240 in 1993 to $73,760 in 1999, $74,810 in 2007 and $85,210 in 2024 in the inspected consistent-dollar series. Long plateaus do not justify the blanket no-growth claim. The series is not individual longitudinal income.

evidence.title: Real Median Household Income in the United States
evidence.finding: Inflation-adjusted median household income in 2025 dollars: 1993 $64,240; 1999 $73,760; 2007 $74,810; 2019 $85,320; 2024 $85,210; 2025 $87,460. Not a longitudinal measure of each household.

claims.next_check: Obtain primary evidence matching the stated metric, period and conditions before assigning an outcome grade.
